# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

response:
# Critical reading of Achterberg et al., meta-analysis of reduced working time

This is a careful review, and most of its conclusions are well calibrated. The protocol was registered, self-rated productivity is excluded, and the subgroups separate exactly the factors that inflated the Halden figure. The authors are frank that design and measurement overlap. The discussion's middle position, a real but modest per-hour gain that depends on work type, fits the earlier papers well.

There is one clear overreach: the claim that novelty "can be set aside." The small-study adjustment also deserves more caution than the paper gives it, and a few reporting gaps matter.

I checked the counts. Every subgroup split adds up to 23 (9+14, 8+15, 12+11, 13+7+3).

## What it does well

- **It weights the two outcomes properly.** Output per worker, not only per hour, is the figure that tells an employer whether the hours cut pays for itself. The paper gives it due weight.
- **The work-type finding is the most solid result in the review.** Coverage-bound work lost about 9% per worker, with low heterogeneity across all 7 studies (I² = 22%). This matches Varden's counter stratum (−11.4%) and Halden's retail results.
- **The controlled discretionary estimate is the most useful single number.** It is +9.6% per hour and −2.7% per worker, across 5 studies. The authors report it rather than leaving the inflated +15.1% unqualified.
- **The response to Varga and Holm is fair.** The controlled, actual-hours and record-based subgroups all avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, and all three still show gains whose intervals exclude zero.
- **It reports a prediction interval (−4% to +34%).** Readers can see how much outcomes vary between settings, not just the average.

## Problems

**1. The duration claim makes the same mistake as Varga and Holm, in the opposite direction.** "Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside" rests on four studies. There are three problems with it.

- **It compares different studies, not the same studies over time.** The four long studies may differ from the rest in design, hours measure or work type. Novelty would show up as a decline within a study, and the paper presents no within-study trajectories.
- **Long follow-up selects for success.** Schemes that went badly were more likely to be dropped before reaching 12 months. That makes them less likely to report long-run results.
- **The interval is too wide to rule out decay.** The 95% CI of 6.2% to 22.4% is consistent with substantial decay from short-run levels. It is also compared against the overall +13.4%, which includes the inflated uncontrolled studies. The right comparison is with controlled, actual-hours studies, whose estimate is about +8%.

The defensible statement is: "no evidence of decay in four studies, but too little data to test it." Varden's 24-month follow-up will be more informative than this subgroup.

**2. Trim-and-fill is unreliable here, and the paper gives a weak reason for the asymmetry.**

- Trim-and-fill performs poorly when heterogeneity is high (I² = 81%). Egger's test with 23 studies has limited power and can be misleading in the same conditions.
- The paper puts the funnel asymmetry down to publication bias. A likelier explanation is that the small studies are the uncontrolled, scheduled-hours, manager-rated pilots, which give larger estimates for the reasons the moderator analysis already identifies. That is a study-quality difference, not missing studies.
- A better test would include the standard error in the meta-regression alongside design and measurement, or run Egger's test within the controlled subgroup only.

The +9.1% adjusted figure happens to match the controlled estimates, but the convergence partly comes from the same studies being counted more than once, as the next point explains.

**3. The four estimates that "converge" overlap.** The controlled (8.2%), actual-hours (7.9%), record-based (9.7%) and bias-adjusted (9.1%) estimates draw largely on the same studies. Their agreement is not four separate confirmations. The paper's own conclusion of 8 to 10% is probably right, but it rests mainly on about 9 controlled studies, not four lines of evidence.

**4. The per-worker results reveal the confounding directly.** The hours measure cannot mechanically change output per worker. Yet the actual-hours studies show −3.9% per worker and the scheduled-hours studies show −0.6%. That 3.3-point gap must come from other differences between the studies, most likely design and output measure. Part of the per-hour gap between actual and scheduled hours (+7.9% vs +16.6%) is therefore confounding, not a correction for measurement. The authors acknowledge the overlap in general, but this is a concrete check they could report.

**5. The size of the hours cut is missing as a moderator.** Inclusion requires a cut of at least 10%. When output holds roughly steady, the per-hour gain grows almost automatically with the size of the cut: a flat output after a 10% cut is about +11% per hour, and after a 20% cut it is +25%. Studies with bigger cuts will show bigger per-hour gains for arithmetic reasons. The size of the reduction should be a moderator, or at least reported for each study.

**6. Coding of Varden and Halden is unclear.**

- **Varden.** It contains both a discretionary and a coverage-bound stratum, and the counts (13+7+3 = 23) imply it was entered as one study. Was it coded "mixed," or entered with a pooled estimate? It is one of only 3 randomised trials, so splitting it into its two strata would matter.
- **Halden.** Did the authors use the reported +23.4%, or the corrected figures from Varga and Holm's re-analysis of the microdata? The paper's rule says to use actual hours where available, and Varga and Holm reported actual hours for 27 organisations. The attrition Halden misreported also needs handling.

**7. There is no formal risk-of-bias assessment.** The paper gives no RoB 2 or ROBINS-I ratings and no GRADE certainty rating. Attrition, as in Halden, and the sponsor's role in measurement are not coded. Many pilots are run or publicised by advocacy organisations, so funding and sponsorship deserve coding too.

**8. Smaller points.**

- **Two different effects are pooled together.** Controlled studies contribute a difference from a comparison group, while uncontrolled studies contribute a change from baseline. These measure different things. Pooling them is common practice but should be flagged, and the moderator analysis only partly deals with it.
- **The variance source is not stated.** Many pilots, Halden among them, report no standard errors, and the paper doesn't say how variances were obtained.
- **Wellbeing results are counted, not estimated.** "Sick leave fell in all 14 studies" is mostly uncontrolled evidence. A controlled-only estimate would be more informative.
- **The mechanism analysis is underpowered.** The fatigue correlation (r = 0.18 across 11 studies) compares study averages and has little power. It is weak evidence against fatigue as a mechanism, not evidence that fatigue doesn't matter. The paper's wording is roughly right, but it should not be read as ruling fatigue out.
- **The work-type cross-tabulation is missing.** It's not reported how work type cross-tabulates with design. If coverage-bound studies are more often controlled public-sector trials, the controlled subgroup's per-worker −4.1% partly reflects which kinds of work it contains.

## Conclusions the evidence supports

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Headline pilot figures above 20% are inflated | Well supported |
| Per-hour gain is about 8–10% in better-designed studies | Supported, mainly by ~9 controlled studies |
| Discretionary work: output per worker roughly maintained (about −3% to 0%) | Supported, modest confidence |
| Coverage-bound work: output per worker falls about 9% | Well supported and consistent |
| Gains are not entirely an artifact | Supported |
| Reduced hours are not sector-general | Supported |
| Effects don't decay / novelty can be set aside | Not supported; the data are too thin |
| Publication bias explains the funnel asymmetry | Uncertain; study quality is a likelier cause |

## Across the four papers

| Paper | Per-hour estimate |
|---|---|
| Halden as reported | +23.4% |
| Varga and Holm corrected subset | +10.8% |
| Varden case-processing | +12.5% |
| Meta-analysis, controlled discretionary | +9.6% |

The estimates converge on roughly 10% per hour in discretionary work, measured properly. That is close to break-even per worker for cuts of about 10–13% in actual hours. Coverage-bound work needs extra staff to hold service levels.

The two biggest open questions are durability and mechanism. Neither the meta-analysis nor the comment has settled them, and both sides overstated their case. Varden's 24-month follow-up and its registered meetings test are the results to watch.
